Training-only graphs can still expose a training example’s own target through transition counts. GCL4SR aggregates transitions across training sequences; its construction does not specify per-example exclusion ([paper](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2022/0333.pdf)). A direct exclusion precedent is IGMC, which removes the queried training edge before prediction ([paper](https://www.cse.wustl.edu/~yixin.chen/public/ICLR.pdf)). I found no clearly established sequential-recommendation method specifically using leave-one-user-out transition features. A defensible adaptation is user-grouped cross-fitting: construct each fold’s graph from other users, train the scorer on excluded users, then use all training users’ graph at inference. Recompute counts, marginals and normalization after exclusion. This extrapolates target-statistic safeguards from [CatBoost](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09516), rather than reproducing a published sequential method.

For sparse edges, neighborhood methods shrink similarity by n/(n+λ), where n is supporting co-observation count ([Desrosiers–Karypis chapter](https://cse.iitk.ac.in/users/nsrivast/HCC/Recommender_systems_handbook.pdf)). An analogous transition design is P̃(j|i)=(cᵢⱼ+αpⱼ)/(cᵢ+α), followed by log-lift log[P̃(j|i)/pⱼ]; optionally shrink that residual by cᵢⱼ/(cᵢⱼ+λ). These formulas are proposed adaptations, not reported findings. Count distinct supporting users to reduce repeated-user domination; tune smoothing using validation only.

Compare against smoothed first-order Markov transitions, FPMC’s user-preference plus factorized-transition score ([original paper](https://www.iw3c2.org/papers/2025-Factorizing-Personalized-Markov-Chains.pdf)), and recency-weighted item-kNN, both standalone and added as a validation-tuned SASRec score residual. Nearest-neighbor methods are serious baselines: a controlled session-recommendation study found them frequently preferable to more complex models ([study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.12781)). This does not establish superiority on these Amazon categories; compare all variants using the pinned macro validation HR@10.
